en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 44.1 (SN 44.1, PTS SN iv 374) 1. The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga) The Discourse to Khemā (Khemāsutta)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Khemā, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, had taken up residence at Toraṇavatthu between Sāvatthī and Sāketa.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, took up a single night’s stay at Toraṇavatthu between Sāketa and Sāvatthī.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man:
“Come, good man, find out in Toraṇavatthu whether there is some ascetic or brahmin such that I might pay him a visit today.
“Yes, sire,” that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala, and having done so, he searched throughout the entire [city].
While wandering about Toranavathu, that man did not see any such ascetic or brahmin whom King Pasenadi of Kosala might visit.
However, he saw the bhikkhunī Khemā who had taken up residence at Toranavathu.
Having seen him, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala; having approached, he said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
"Your Majesty, there is no such ascetic or brahmin in Toraṇavatthu whom Your Majesty might attend upon.
However, Your Majesty, there is a bhikkhunī named Khemā, a disciple of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
"Moreover, this noble lady has acquired such a fine reputation:
'She is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, eloquent, and possessed of excellent presence of mind.
Let Your Majesty attend upon her."
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the bhikkhunī Khemā;
having approached, he paid homage to the bhikkhunī Khemā and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the bhikkhunī Khemā:
“Venerable lady, does the Tathāgata exist after death?
“Great King, this has not been declared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata exists after death.’”
“But, lady, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
“Great King, this too has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death.’”
“But what, noble lady, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
“This, Great King, was left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
“But, lady, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
“Great King, this too has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
“When you were asked, ‘Venerable lady, does the Tathāgata exist after death?’, being thus questioned, you said:
‘This has not been declared by the Blessed One, Great King—
that the Tathāgata exists after death.’”
“But when asked, ‘But then, lady, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
you replied, ‘This too, Great King, was left undeclared by the Blessed One:
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death.”’”
“When you were asked, ‘Venerable lady, does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
you replied: ‘This has been left undeclared by the Blessed One, Great King—that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’”
“But when asked, ‘Lady, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
you replied, ‘This too, Great King, has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
“What, noble lady, is the cause, what is the reason why this has not been explained by the Blessed One?
“In that case, Great King, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer it as you see fit.
What do you think, Great King?”
"Do you have any accountant, calculator, or mathematician who is able to count the sands of the Ganges, saying:

'There are this many grains of sand,' or 'There are this many hundreds of grains of sand,' or 'There are this many thousands of grains of sand,' or 'There are this many hundreds of thousands of grains of sand'?
"Certainly not, Noble Lady."
“But do you have any accountant, calculator, or mathematician who is able to count the water in the great ocean— saying,

‘there are this many āḷhakas of water,’ or ‘there are this many hundreds of āḷhakas of water,’ or ‘there are this many thousands of āḷhakas of water,’ or ‘there are this many hundreds of thousands of āḷhakas of water’?
“Certainly not, noble lady.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, noble lady, the great ocean is deep, immeasurable, and difficult to fathom.

“In the same way, Great King, whatever form by which one might define the Tathāgata has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.”
“Great king, the Tathāgata is liberated from reckoning in terms of form; he is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, like the great ocean.
It does not apply that ‘the Tathāgata exists after death,’ nor does it apply that ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death.’”

He does not enter into the position that "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," nor does he enter into the position that "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.

Whatever feeling one might use to designate the Tathāgata, that feeling has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to future non-arising.
"Released from the conceptualization of feeling, Great King, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom—
just like the great ocean.
The notion that 'the Tathāgata exists after death' does not apply, nor does the notion that 'the Tathāgata does not exist after death'."

One does not arrive at the position that "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," nor does one arrive at the position that "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
By means of whatever perception [one might conceive] regarding the Tathāgata... [and so forth].

Those formations by which one might describe the Tathāgata have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.
Released from reckoning as formations, Great King, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable— just like the great ocean.
‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ does not apply; ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death’ does not apply;
‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply;
‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.

That consciousness by which one might designate a Tathāgata has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
Released from the reckoning of consciousness, Great King, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, just like the great ocean.

"It does not apply that 'the Tathāgata exists after death,' nor does it apply that 'the Tathāgata does not exist after death,' nor does it apply that 'the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' nor does it apply that 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.'"

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Bhikkhunī Khemā’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Bhikkhunī Khemā, and keeping her to his right, departed.
Then, at a later time, King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala...
He said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, does the Tathāgata exist after death?
“This, great king, has not been declared by me: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death.’”
‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death?
“But, venerable sir, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
“This too, great king, has been left undeclared by me:”
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death.
“But, Bhante, does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? “This, Great King, has been left undeclared by me: ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’”
“‘Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
“But, Bhante, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
“This too, Great King, has been left undeclared by me: ‘Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?’”
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
[The king asked: “Venerable sir, when you were asked, ‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death?
you replied: ‘This, Great King, has been left undeclared by me—that the Tathāgata exists after death…’” [and so on].
“But, venerable sir, when asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death? you say:
‘This too, great king, has been left undeclared by me:
that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why this has not been declared by the Blessed One?
“In that case, great king, I shall question you about this very matter. You may answer it as you see fit.
What do you think, great king: is there any accountant, calculator, or mathematician who is able to count the grains of sand in the Ganges?”
“Or ‘there are this many grains of sand,’ or even ‘there are this many hundreds of thousands of grains of sand’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“But is there any accountant, calculator, or mathematician who is able to count the water in the great ocean—”
“...or ‘there are this many hundreds of thousands of water-measures’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“And what is the reason for that?”
“Great, Bhante, is the ocean, deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom.

Even so, Great King, whatever form by which one might designate the Tathāgata has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Released from the category of form, Great King, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom.”
Just as with the great ocean:
"The Tathāgata exists after death"—this does not apply; ...pe...
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—this also does not apply.
Whatever feeling...
whatever perception... whatever mental formations...

whatever consciousness by which one might designate a Tathāgata—that consciousness has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
“Great king, the Tathāgata is liberated from the category of consciousness; he is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, just like the great ocean.
It does not apply that ‘the Tathāgata exists after death,’ nor does it apply that ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death.’”
“He does not apply himself to the view: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’; he does not apply himself to the view: ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’;
nor does he apply himself to the view: ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!”
For indeed, where the meaning and the phrasing of both the Teacher and his disciple coincide, harmonize, and do not contradict one another—
namely, regarding the supreme state— on one occasion, venerable sir, I approached the bhikkhunī Khemā and asked her about this matter.
That noble lady also explained the matter to me using these very words and these very phrases, just as the Blessed One has done.
"It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How the meaning of the Teacher and the meaning of his disciple coincide, how their phrasing coincides, and how they do not conflict with one another regarding this supreme state!
Come now, Bhante, we shall depart."
“We have many duties and much to do.
“Then, Great King, depart at whatever time you deem fit.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.

The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga)
The Anurādha Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Anurādha was dwelling not far from the Blessed One in a forest hut.
Then a number of wanderers of other sects approached the Venerable Anurādha. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Anurādha.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said this to the Venerable Anurādha:
“Friend Anurādha, when the Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—is described by the Tathāgata in these four ways:

‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—is he described by the Tathāgata in these four ways?”
“Friends, when a Tathāgata—who is a supreme person, a superlative person, one who has attained the highest attainment—is described by a Tathāgata, he is described apart from these four positions:

‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
When this was said, those wanderers of other sects said this to the Venerable Anurādha:
“Perhaps this bhikkhu is new, having recently gone forth, or perhaps he is an elder who is foolish and incompetent.
Then those wanderers of other sects, having disparaged the Venerable Anurādha with the terms “new” and “foolish,” rose from their seats and departed.
Not long after those wanderers of other sects had left, it occurred to the Venerable Anurādha:
“If those wanderers of other sects were to question me further,
how should I answer them so that I would be speaking the word of the Blessed One,
not misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is false, and in accordance with the Dhamma?”
“...and no legitimate criticism or reproach would find ground for censure?

Then the Venerable Anurādha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Anurādha said this to the Blessed One:
“Just now, Bhante, I was dwelling in a forest hut not far from the Blessed One.”
Then, venerable sir, a number of wanderers of other sects approached me; having approached, they exchanged greetings with me.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, venerable sir, those wanderers of other sects said this to me:
"Friend Anurādha, regarding that Tathāgata, the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—that Tathāgata, when describing him, describes him in these four ways:..."
“‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death’ … or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?
When this was said, Bhante, I said this to those wanderers of other sects:
“Friends, when a Tathāgata— such a supreme person, such a highest person, who has attained the highest attainment— is described by a Tathāgata, he describes him apart from these four positions:
‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or … [as before] … ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
When this was said, venerable sir, those wanderers of other sects said this to me:
“That bhikkhu must be a newcomer, one who has not long gone forth, or perhaps an elder who is foolish and incompetent.
Then, venerable sir, after discouraging me with their talk of being a newcomer and their talk of being foolish, those wanderers of other sects rose from their seats and departed.
"Venerable sir, not long after those wanderers of other sects had departed, this thought occurred to me:
'If those wanderers of other sects were to question me further,
how should I answer them so that I would both speak as they have been instructed and yet not misrepresent the Blessed One?'"
“...and would I thus misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, would I explain in accordance with the Dhamma,
and would no reasonable criticism or rebuttal find ground for censure?
“What do you think, Anurādha?”
“Is form permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Is feeling permanent or impermanent? … [and so on] …
“Is perception …pe… are volitional formations …pe… is consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Therefore, Anurādha, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
Whatever feeling there is— past, future, or present … whatever perception there is … whatever mental formations there are … [and so forth].
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."

Seeing thus, Anurādha, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises:
"It is liberated. He understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
“What do you think, Anurādha,
do you regard form as the Tathāgata?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Do you regard feeling as the Tathāgata?
“No, venerable sir.
“Do you regard perception as the Tathāgata?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Do you regard volitional formations as the Tathāgata?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Do you regard consciousness as the Tathāgata?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Anurādha?”
"Do you regard the Tathāgata as being in form?
"No indeed, Bhante.
"Do you regard the Tathāgata as being apart from form?"
“No, venerable sir.
“Feeling … [and so on] … apart from feeling …”
In perception … [and so on] … apart from perception … [and so on] … in volitional formations … [and so on] …
“Do you regard the Tathāgata as being apart from volitional formations … [and so on] … as being in consciousness?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Do you regard the Tathāgata as being apart from consciousness?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“What do you think, Anurādha?”
“Do you regard form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as the Tathāgata?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“What do you think, Anurādha?”
“Do you regard him as the Tathāgata who is formless, without feeling, without perception, without volitional formations, and without consciousness?
“No, venerable sir.
“In that case, Anurādha, since the Tathāgata is not found by you here in this very life in truth and reality, is it appropriate for you to make such a declaration?”
"Friends, when that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—is described by the Tathāgata apart from these four positions, how does he describe him?
Does he describe him as 'the Tathāgata exists after death'...
or as 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'?"
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, good, Anurādha!
Both formerly and now, Anurādha, it is only suffering that I proclaim, and the cessation of suffering.”

The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga)
The First Sāriputta-Koṭṭhika Sutta On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, does the Tathāgata exist after death?
"This, friend, has not been declared by the Blessed One."
“‘Does the Tathāgata exist after death?
“But, friend, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
“This too, friend, has been left undeclared by the Blessed One.”
“‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death.
“But, friend, does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
“This, friend, has been left undeclared by the Blessed One.”
“‘Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
“But, friend, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
“This too, friend, has been left undeclared by the Blessed One.”
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
“When asked, ‘Friend, does the Tathāgata exist after death? you say, ‘This has been left undeclared by the Blessed One—that the Tathāgata exists after death. … [and so on] …”
“But when asked, ‘Friend, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death? you say:
‘This too, friend, has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
“What, friends, is the cause, what is the reason why this has not been declared by the Blessed One?
“‘A Tathāgata exists after death,’ friend, is a matter pertaining to form.
‘A Tathāgata does not exist after death’ is a matter pertaining to form.”
“The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death”—this pertains to form.
“The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death”—this pertains to form.
“The Tathāgata exists after death,” friend, this pertains to feeling.
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death"—this pertains to feeling.
"The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death"—this pertains to feeling.
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—this pertains to feeling.
"Friend, 'The Tathāgata exists after death'—this is a mere perception.
'The Tathāgata does not exist after death'—this is a mere perception.
'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death'—this is a mere perception."
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—this is a mode of perception.
‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ friend, this is a mode of conditioned phenomena.
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ this is a mode of conditioned phenomena.
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’—this belongs to the realm of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—this belongs to the realm of conditioned formations.
‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ friend, this belongs to the realm of consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
"The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
“This, friends, is the cause, this is the reason why this was left undeclared by the Blessed One.
The third [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 44.4 (SN 44.4, PTS SN iv 386)

1. The Chapter on the Indeterminate. The Second Discourse with Sāriputta and Koṭṭhita. At one time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana... [as before] ... The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and cordial greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, it was said: ‘The indeterminate, the indeterminate. To what extent, friend, is something called ‘indeterminate’? “Friend Koṭṭhita, that which is not conducive to enlightenment, does not lead to enlightenment, and does not conduce to the complete destruction of suffering—that is called ‘indeterminate. “But, friend Sāriputta, what is not conducive to enlightenment, does not lead to enlightenment, and does not conduce to the complete destruction of suffering? “Friend Koṭṭhita, wrong view is not conducive to enlightenment, does not lead to enlightenment, and does not conduce to the complete destruction of suffering. Wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration are not conducive to enlightenment, do not lead to enlightenment, and do not conduce to the complete destruction of suffering. These, friend Koṭṭhita, are called ‘indeterminate. “Friend Sāriputta, it was said: ‘The determinate, the determinate. To what extent, friend, is something called ‘determinate’? “Friend Koṭṭhita, that which is conducive to enlightenment, leads to enlightenment, and conduces to the complete destruction of suffering—that is called ‘determinate. “But, friend Sāriputta, what is conducive to enlightenment, leads to enlightenment, and conduces to the complete destruction of suffering? “Friend Koṭṭhita, right view is conducive to enlightenment, leads to enlightenment, and conduces to the complete destruction of suffering. Right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are conducive to enlightenment, lead to enlightenment, and conduce to the complete destruction of suffering. These, friend Koṭṭhita, are called ‘determinate. “It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta! It is marvelous, friend Sāriputta! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Sāriputta: ‘That which is not conducive to enlightenment... is called “indeterminate. That which is conducive to enlightenment... is called “determinate. “It is wonderful, friend Koṭṭhita! It is marvelous, friend Koṭṭhita! How well this has been understood by the Venerable Koṭṭhita! Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta. Delighted, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita rejoiced in what the Venerable Sāriputta had said. This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said. Elated, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Sāriputta. At one time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana... [as before] ... [The discourse continues as above. This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said. Elated, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Sāriputta. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bound in both ways; the person who is bound by the fetter of lust; the person who is bound by the fetter of views; and the person who is liberated in both ways. And how, bhikkhus, is a person bound in both ways? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has not abandoned sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty, and has not abandoned the underlying tendencies to sensual desire, existence, and ignorance. This, bhikkhus, is called a person bound in both ways. And how, bhikkhus, is a person bound by the fetter of lust? ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ this occurs to him; ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ this occurs to him.

"Friend, for one who delights in perception...

‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ or ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ or ‘the soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’
‘Or that a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or even ‘That a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
For in this matter, the meaning of the Teacher and the meaning of the disciple coincide, their phrasing coincides, and they do not conflict with one another regarding this supreme state.”
"Just now, Master Gotama, I approached the ascetic Mahāmoggallāna and asked him about this matter.
The ascetic Moggallāna also explained that matter to me using these very same terms and phrases, just as Master Gotama has done.
It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!"

"For indeed, where the meaning of the Teacher and the meaning of the disciple coincide, and the phrasing of the Teacher and the phrasing of the disciple coincide, and they do not conflict with one another—namely, regarding the supreme state.
Thus ends the seventh [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 44.8 (SN 44.8, PTS SN iv 395).
1. The Chapter on the Indeterminate.
The Discourse to Vacchagotta.
Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, is the world eternal?
"This has not been declared by me, Vaccha: 'The world is eternal'... [and so on].
“But, Master Gotama, is it the case that ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?
“Vaccha, this too has been left undeclared by me:
‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
“Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why wanderers of other sects, when asked thus, give such an explanation:
‘The world is eternal,’ or … [as before] … ‘A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”
"But what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why when you are asked thus, you do not give such an answer as:
'The world is eternal'...
[or] 'A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'?"
“Vaccha, the wanderers of other sects regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
They regard feeling as self … perception as self …” [and so on].
They regard volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as being in self, or self as being in volitional formations. Therefore,
when wanderers of other sects are questioned thus, their answer is as follows:
‘The world is eternal,’ or …pe… ‘A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
And yet, Vaccha, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.
One does not regard feeling as self … [and so on] … one does not regard perception … [and so on] … one does not regard volitional formations … [and so on].
One does not regard consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as being in self, nor self as being in consciousness.
Therefore, when asked thus, the Tathāgata does not give such an explanation:
"The world is eternal," and so forth...
“...nor that ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
Then the wanderer Vacchagotta rose from his seat and approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.

‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.

Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.

“Master Gotama, in earlier days, even much earlier, when many ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of various sects were sitting together and assembled in the Hall of Wonders, this discussion arose among them:
‘This Pūraṇa Kassapa is indeed the head of an order, the leader of a group, the teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect, and esteemed as holy by the multitude.
He too declares the rebirth of a disciple who has passed away and died:’”
“Such-and-such a person has been reborn there; such-and-such a person has been reborn there.

And regarding his disciple who was a supreme person, a most excellent person, one who had attained the highest attainment—even that disciple, when he has passed away and died, he declares his rebirths:
“Such-and-such a person has been reborn there; such-and-such a person has been reborn there.”
This Makkhali Gosāla as well...
[as before] ...this Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta as well...
[as before] ...this Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta as well... [as before] ...
This Pakudha Kaccāyana...
[and so on] ...this Ajita Kesakambala is also a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect esteemed as holy by many people.
He too declares the rebirths of a disciple who has passed away and died:
‘That one has been reborn there, that one has been reborn there.
And regarding his disciple who is a supreme person, a most excellent person, one who has attained the highest attainment—when that disciple has passed away and died, he declares their rebirth:
‘That one has been reborn there, that one has been reborn there.’”
This ascetic Gotama is also a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group, renowned and famous, a founder of a sect esteemed as holy by many people.
He too declares the rebirths of his disciples who have passed away and died:
"So-and-so has been reborn there; so-and-so has been reborn there."

that one was reborn there.
Rather, he declares it in this way:
‘He has cut off craving, he has turned away the fetters, and through the perfect realization of conceit, he has made an end of suffering.

‘How indeed could the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama be directly known?’”
“Enough, Vaccha, of being perplexed; enough of being doubtful.

For I declare rebirth for one who has grasping, Vaccha, not for one without grasping.”
“Just as, Vaccha, a fire burns with fuel,

“Vaccha, at whatever time a flame is carried far away by the wind, I designate that as having the wind as its fuel.

“But, Master Gotama, when a being lays down this body and has not yet been reborn in another body, what does Master Gotama designate as its fuel?”
“Vaccha, at whatever time one lays down this body and a being has not yet been reborn in another body, I call that craving the fuel.
For at that time, Vaccha, craving is indeed the fuel. Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, does the self exist?"

“But, Master Gotama, does the self not exist?

"Why, Bhante, did the Blessed One not provide an answer when asked a question by the wanderer Vacchagotta?"
“Ānanda, if, when asked by the wanderer Vacchagotta whether ‘the self exists,’ I were to answer ‘the self exists,’ that would be in agreement with those recluses and brahmins who hold to eternalism.

‘All phenomena are non-self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”

“Ānanda, if I, when asked by the wanderer Vacchagotta whether there is no self, were to answer ‘there is no self,’ that would lead to further confusion for the already confused wanderer Vacchagotta, who might think:

Saṁyutta Nikāya 44.11 (SN 44.11, PTS SN iv 401) 1. The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga) The Discourse to Sabhiya Kaccāna At Sāvatthī. There, the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna addressed the Blessed One thus: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “It is not easy, Sabhiya, for one who has not seen this Dhamma to understand it through a brief instruction. However, I shall give you a brief teaching; having understood its meaning, you should practice accordingly. “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit? “Sabhiya, when one sees form as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,’ then, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit. When one sees feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,’ then, in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one sees form as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’? How does one see feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’? “Sabhiya, when one sees eye and forms as they really are with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’; when one sees ear and sounds... nose and odors... tongue and tastes... body and tangibles... mind and mental phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—then, Sabhiya, one knows and sees thus, and in regard to this body with its consciousness and all external phenomena, there is no more I-making, mine-making, or the underlying tendency to conceit. When this was said, the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. On one occasion the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna was staying at Ñatika in the Brick House.
Then the wanderer Vacchagotta approached the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna:
“Venerable Kaccāna, does the Tathāgata exist after death?
“Vaccha, this has not been declared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata exists after death.’”
“But, Master Kaccāna, does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
“Vaccha, this too has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death.’”
“Venerable Kaccāna, does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
“Vaccha, this has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’”
“But, Master Kaccāna, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?
“Vaccha, this too has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’”
“When asked, ‘Venerable Kaccāna, does the Tathāgata exist after death?
you replied, ‘Vaccha, this has not been declared by the Blessed One:
“The Tathāgata exists after death.”’”
"But, Master Kaccāna, when asked: 'Does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
you replied: 'This has not been declared by the Blessed One, Vaccha—that the Tathāgata does not exist after death.'"
“When you were asked, ‘Venerable Kaccāna, does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
you replied, ‘Vaccha, this has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’”
“But, Master Kaccāna, when asked: ‘Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?’—being thus questioned, you say:
‘This too, Vaccha, has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
“The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.”’”
“Master Kaccāna, what is the cause, what is the reason, why this has not been declared by the ascetic Gotama?
“Vaccha, whatever is the cause and whatever is the reason for designating one as ‘possessing form,’ or ‘formless,’ or ‘percipient,’ or ‘non-percipient,’ or ‘neither percipient nor non-percipient’—
that cause and that reason exist entirely, in every way, and in all respects.”
"It would cease without remainder.
By means of what could one describe it, describing it as 'possessing form' or 'formless,' or 'percipient,' or 'non-percipient,' or 'neither percipient nor non-percipient'?
"How long has it been since you went forth, Master Kaccāna?"
“Not long, friend—it has been three years.
“Friend, for one who sees it thus, even that much would be a great deal; what need is there to speak of such a long duration as this?
The eleventh [sutta].
The first chapter, on the Undeclared, is concluded.
Its summary verse is:
The Elder Nun Khemā, Anurādha, ...
Sāriputta is Koṭṭhika;
Moggallāna, Vaccha,
Kutūhalasālā, and Ānanda.
The eleventh, Sabhiya.
The *Abyākata-saṃyutta* is complete. Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
The six sense-bases and feeling,
the woman, the jackal-eater;
Sāmaṇḍaka and Moggallāna.
Citta, Gāmaṇi, the conditioned,
and the undeclared— these are the ten.
The fourth chapter, the Saḷāyatana-vagga, is concluded.
The Saṃyutta Nikāya Discourse Collection on the Chapter of the Six Sense Bases is finished.
